claim: Trypanosoma brucei survival depends upon switches in its protective Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) coat by antigenic variation.
source: Survival of Trypanosoma brucei depends upon switches in its protective Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) coat by antigenic variation.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific knowledge about T. brucei biology.

claim: VSG switching occurs by frequent homologous recombination.
source: VSG switching occurs by frequent homologous recombination, which is thought to require locus-specific initiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: RECQ2 acts to repair DNA breaks, including in the telomeric site of VSG expression.
source: Here, we show that a RecQ helicase, RECQ2, acts to repair DNA breaks, including in the telomeric site of VSG expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including clonal survival assays and I-SceI induction experiments.

claim: RECQ2 loss does not impair antigenic variation.
source: Despite this, RECQ2 loss does not impair antigenic variation, but causes increased VSG switching by recombination
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data presented in Figure 4.

claim: RECQ2 loss causes increased VSG switching by recombination.
source: Despite this, RECQ2 loss does not impair antigenic variation, but causes increased VSG switching by recombination
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing elevated switching rates in recq2-/- mutants (Figure 4).

claim: DSBs inefficiently direct recombination in the VSG expression site.
source: Indeed, we show DSBs inefficiently direct recombination in the VSG expression site.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing inefficient repair after I-SceI induction in HRES cells (Figure 5).

claim: The transcribed VSG expression site is the only telomeric site that is early replicating.
source: By mapping genome replication dynamics, we reveal that the transcribed VSG expression site is the only telomeric site that is early replicating – a differential timing only seen in mammal-infective parasites.
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data showing early replication of BES1 in BSF cells but not PCF cells (Figure 7).

claim: Differential replication timing of the active VSG expression site is only seen in mammal-infective parasites.
source: By mapping genome replication dynamics, we reveal that the transcribed VSG expression site is the only telomeric site that is early replicating – a differential timing only seen in mammal-infective parasites.
evidence: This is supported by comparing MFAseq data between BSF and PCF cells (Figure 7).

claim: There is a specific association between VSG transcription and replication timing.
source: Specific association between VSG transcription and replication timing reveals a model for antigenic variation based on replication-derived DNA fragility.
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq and qPCR data showing early replication correlates with transcription status (Figures 7 and 8).

claim: Antigenic variation is based on replication-derived DNA fragility.
source: Specific association between VSG transcription and replication timing reveals a model for antigenic variation based on replication-derived DNA fragility.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the inference from the replication timing data and VSG switching observations.

claim: T. brucei employs two distinct approaches for antigenic variation: recombination and transcription.
source: In this regard, antigenic variation in the African trypanosome, Trypanosoma brucei, is unusual, since here two apparently distinct approaches are adopted: recombination and transcription.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field about T. brucei antigenic variation mechanisms.

claim: The VSG protein forms a dense coat that shields invariant antigens from immune recognition.
source: Antigenic variation in T. brucei involves switches in the identity of the Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) expressed on the cell surface, where the protein forms a dense 'coat' that is believed to shield invariant antigens from immune recognition (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: An individual T. brucei cell in the mammal expresses only one VSG gene at any given time.
source: At any given time an individual T. brucei cell in the mammal expresses only one VSG gene, due to transcriptional control mechanisms that ensure only one of ~15 VSG transcription sites, termed bloodstream expression sites (BES), is active.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei VSG expression.

claim: Only one of ~15 VSG transcription sites (BES) is active at a time.
source: At any given time an individual T. brucei cell in the mammal expresses only one VSG gene, due to transcriptional control mechanisms that ensure only one of ~15 VSG transcription sites, termed bloodstream expression sites (BES), is active.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei BES expression.

claim: Monoallelic expression is found in other antigenic variation systems, such as that involving the ~60 var genes in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Such monoallelic expression is found in other antigenic variation systems, such as that involving the ~60 var genes in Plasmodium falciparum (Guizetti and Scherf, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guizetti and Scherf, 2013.

claim: The BES has an elaborate structure where the VSG is co-transcribed with many other genes (ESAGs) from an RNA Polymerase I promoter.
source: One complexity in understanding VSG transcriptional switching is the elaborate structure of the BES (Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008), where the VSG is co-transcribed with many other genes, termed expression site-associated genes (ESAGs), from an RNA Polymerase I promoter.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008.

claim: The VSG is always proximal to the telomere in all BES.
source: Despite some variation in ESAG composition between BES, two features appear invariant in all these sites: the VSG is always proximal to the telomere and is separated from the upstream ESAGs by an array of 70 bp repeats (which appear to be only found adjacent to VSGs in the T. brucei genome)(Marcello and Barry, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: The VSG is separated from upstream ESAGs by an array of 70 bp repeats in all BES.
source: Despite some variation in ESAG composition between BES, two features appear invariant in all these sites: the VSG is always proximal to the telomere and is separated from the upstream ESAGs by an array of 70 bp repeats (which appear to be only found adjacent to VSGs in the T. brucei genome)(Marcello and Barry, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: 70 bp repeats appear to be only found adjacent to VSGs in the T. brucei genome.
source: Despite some variation in ESAG composition between BES, two features appear invariant in all these sites: the VSG is always proximal to the telomere and is separated from the upstream ESAGs by an array of 70 bp repeats (which appear to be only found adjacent to VSGs in the T. brucei genome)(Marcello and Barry, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: Recombination is the major route for VSG switching in numerical terms.
source: However, a second route of VSG switching relies upon recombination and can over-write the BES-resident VSGs, generating new VSG coats from a genomic archive of ~2000 VSGs (Cross et al., 2014; Marcello and Barry, 2007). In numerical terms, therefore, recombination is the major route for VSG switching.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cross et al., 2014 and Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: The VSG archive contains ~2000 VSGs.
source: However, a second route of VSG switching relies upon recombination and can over-write the BES-resident VSGs, generating new VSG coats from a genomic archive of ~2000 VSGs (Cross et al., 2014; Marcello and Barry, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cross et al., 2014 and Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: Recombination is a very widespread strategy for antigenic variation in eukaryotic and bacterial pathogens.
source: Indeed, recombination is a very widespread strategy for antigenic variation in eukaryotic and bacterial pathogens (Palmer and Brayton, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Palmer and Brayton, 2007.

claim: Recombination drives antigen diversity, which prolongs infection and facilitates transmission.
source: Indeed, recombination is a very widespread strategy for antigenic variation in eukaryotic and bacterial pathogens (Palmer and Brayton, 2007), most likely because it drives antigen diversity, which prolongs infection and facilitates transmission (Hall et al., 2013; Mugnier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2013 and Mugnier et al., 2015.

claim: The VSG archive is distributed across three chromosome classes in the T. brucei nuclear genome.
source: The VSG archive is distributed across the three chromosome classes that comprise the T. brucei nuclear genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei genome organization.

claim: BES are found in the 11 diploid megabase chromosomes and in the ~5 aneuploid intermediate chromosomes.
source: A small part of the archive is the BES (Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008), which are found in the 11 diploid megabase chromosomes as well as in the ~5 aneuploid intermediate chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008.

claim: A larger part of the VSG archive is found at the telomeres of ~100 minichromosomes.
source: A larger part of the archive is found at the telomeres of ~100 minichromosomes (Wickstead et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wickstead et al., 2004.

claim: ESAGs and BES promoters have not been found at minichromosome telomeres.
source: A larger part of the archive is found at the telomeres of ~100 minichromosomes (Wickstead et al., 2004), where ESAGs and BES promoters have not been found, suggesting this part of the archive is simply a store of silent VSGs for recombination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wickstead et al., 2004 and inference from the absence of these elements.

claim: The largest silent VSG store is composed of arrays of VSGs in the subtelomeres of the megabase chromosomes.
source: The largest silent store is composed of arrays of VSGs in the subtelomeres of the megabase chromosomes, where the majority of the VSGs are pseudogenes or partial genes (Berriman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berriman et al., 2005.

claim: The majority of VSGs in subtelomeric arrays are pseudogenes or partial genes.
source: The largest silent store is composed of arrays of VSGs in the subtelomeres of the megabase chromosomes, where the majority of the VSGs are pseudogenes or partial genes (Berriman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berriman et al., 2005.

claim: Reciprocal VSG recombination involves telomere exchange between two chromosomes.
source: A minor route for switching is termed reciprocal VSG recombination, where telomeres are exchanged between two chromosomes, moving the VSG out of the active BES and moving a previously silent VSG into the active BES (Rudenko et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rudenko et al., 1996.

claim: VSG gene conversion involves deletion of the VSG in the BES and replacement by VSG sequence copied from the silent archive.
source: More common is VSG gene conversion, which can involve both intact and impaired VSGs, and involves deletion of the VSG in the BES and replacement by VSG sequence copied from the silent archive.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VSG gene conversion mechanisms.

claim: Early in infections gene conversion of intact VSGs predominates.
source: Early in infections gene conversion of intact VSGs predominates (Marcello and Barry, 2007; Morrison et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcello and Barry, 2007 and Morrison et al., 2005.

claim: ~90% of VSGs are flanked by 70 bp repeats.
source: ~90% of VSGs are flanked by 70 bp repeats (Marcello and Barry, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcello and Barry, 2007.

claim: 70 bp repeats provide upstream homology to guide recombination of virtually all genes in the VSG archive.
source: ~90% of VSGs are flanked by 70 bp repeats (Marcello and Barry, 2007), which provide upstream homology to guide recombination of virtually all genes in the archive.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marcello and Barry, 2007 and inference about the function of these repeats.

claim: Impaired VSGs are seen as recombination substrates later in infections.
source: Impaired VSGs are seen as recombination substrates later in infections and here gene conversion differs from intact VSGs, since the reaction involves the production of a functional gene using homology within the ORF
evidence: This is established knowledge about the temporal dynamics of VSG recombination.

claim: Multiple VSG donors are frequently recombined to generate novel 'mosaic' VSGs in segmental gene conversion.
source: indeed, multiple VSG donors are frequently recombined to generate novel 'mosaic' VSGs in a reaction termed segmental gene conversion (Hall et al., 2013; Mugnier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2013 and Mugnier et al., 2015.

claim: Switching of intact VSGs by recombination is catalyzed by homologous recombination (HR).
source: All available evidence suggests switching of intact VSGs by recombination is catalyzed by homologous recombination (HR), a universally conserved reaction that directs repair of DNA damage and maintains replication fork progression genome-wide.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of RAD51 impairs but does not abolish VSG recombination, including gene conversion.
source: Mutation of the central catalytic enzyme of HR, RAD51, impairs (but does not abolish) VSG recombination, including gene conversion (McCulloch and Barry, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCulloch and Barry, 1999.

claim: Mutation of T. brucei BRCA2 impairs VSG recombination.
source: Consistent with that phenotype, mutation of T. brucei BRCA2 (Hartley and McCulloch, 2008) and at least one of four RAD51 paralogues (Dobson et al., 2011) - factors that aid RAD51 function - has the same outcome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hartley and McCulloch, 2008.

claim: Mutation of at least one of four RAD51 paralogues impairs VSG recombination.
source: Consistent with that phenotype, mutation of T. brucei BRCA2 (Hartley and McCulloch, 2008) and at least one of four RAD51 paralogues (Dobson et al., 2011) - factors that aid RAD51 function - has the same outcome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dobson et al., 2011.

claim: Mutation of TOP3α results in increased VSG switching that is RAD51-dependent.
source: More recently, mutation of TOP3α or RMI1, which interact and may be components of the T. brucei RTR (RecQ/Sgs1-Top3/TOPO3α- Rmi1/BLAP75/18) complex (Mankouri and Hickson, 2007), was shown to result in increased VSG switching, an effect that is RAD51-dependent (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: Mutation of RMI1 results in increased VSG switching that is RAD51-dependent.
source: More recently, mutation of TOP3α or RMI1, which interact and may be components of the T. brucei RTR (RecQ/Sgs1-Top3/TOPO3α- Rmi1/BLAP75/18) complex (Mankouri and Hickson, 2007), was shown to result in increased VSG switching, an effect that is RAD51-dependent (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: HR genes implicated in VSG switching also function in pilin antigenic variation in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
source: The conclusion that antigenic variation can be executed by a non-specific, general repair pathway is not limited to T. brucei, as similar gene knockout studies in Neisseria gonorrhoeae implicate HR in pilin antigenic variation (Cahoon and Seifert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cahoon and Seifert, 2011.

claim: VSG switching can occur at rates substantially higher than might be predicted for background mutation.
source: However, VSG switching can occur at rates substantially higher than might be predicted for background mutation (Turner, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turner, 1997.

claim: VSG switching may be focused to target the active BES.
source: However, VSG switching can occur at rates substantially higher than might be predicted for background mutation (Turner, 1997) and may be focused to target the active BES, features that may suggest some mechanistic specialization or locus-specificity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on observations in the field.

claim: Controlled induction of I-SceI to generate a DSB adjacent to the 70 bp repeats in the active BES leads to a ~250 fold increase in VSG switching by recombination.
source: First, controlled induction of the endonuclease I-SceI to specifically generate a DSB adjacent to the 70 bp in the active BES leads to a ~250 fold increase in VSG switching by recombination (Boothroyd et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boothroyd et al., 2009.

claim: A DSB induced in other locations in the active BES does not lead to increased VSG switching.
source: First, controlled induction of the endonuclease I-SceI to specifically generate a DSB adjacent to the 70 bp in the active BES leads to a ~250 fold increase in VSG switching by recombination (Boothroyd et al., 2009), an effect not seen when a DSB is induced in other locations in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009; Glover et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boothroyd et al., 2009 and Glover et al., 2013.

claim: Deletion of the 70 bp repeats from the active BES prevents increased VSG switching after DSB induction.
source: First, controlled induction of the endonuclease I-SceI to specifically generate a DSB adjacent to the 70 bp in the active BES leads to a ~250 fold increase in VSG switching by recombination (Boothroyd et al., 2009), an effect not seen when a DSB is induced in other locations in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009; Glover et al., 2013) or when the 70 bp repeats have been deleted from the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boothroyd et al., 2009.

claim: Ligation-mediated PCR can detect DNA breaks in the BES.
source: Second, ligation-mediated PCR is able detect DNA breaks in the BES, with the lesions initially reported to be limited to the vicinity of the 70 bp repeats in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009), though later also reported in the silent BES (Glover et al., 2013; Jehi et al., 2014) and found to be more widely distributed in the transcription units (Glover et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boothroyd et al., 2009, Glover et al., 2013, and Jehi et al., 2014.

claim: DNA breaks were initially reported to be limited to the vicinity of the 70 bp repeats in the active BES.
source: Second, ligation-mediated PCR is able detect DNA breaks in the BES, with the lesions initially reported to be limited to the vicinity of the 70 bp repeats in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boothroyd et al., 2009.

claim: DNA breaks were later reported in the silent BES.
source: Second, ligation-mediated PCR is able detect DNA breaks in the BES, with the lesions initially reported to be limited to the vicinity of the 70 bp repeats in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009), though later also reported in the silent BES (Glover et al., 2013; Jehi et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glover et al., 2013 and Jehi et al., 2014.

claim: DNA breaks in the BES are more widely distributed in the transcription units.
source: Second, ligation-mediated PCR is able detect DNA breaks in the BES, with the lesions initially reported to be limited to the vicinity of the 70 bp repeats in the active BES (Boothroyd et al., 2009), though later also reported in the silent BES (Glover et al., 2013; Jehi et al., 2014) and found to be more widely distributed in the transcription units (Glover et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glover et al., 2013.

claim: TbRECQ2 contains a conserved DEAD/DEAH box helicase domain.
source: Protein domain predictions (Figure 1A) suggest that TbRECQ2 contains a conserved DEAD/DEAH box helicase domain, indicating potential ATP and nucleic acid binding activity
evidence: This is supported by protein domain prediction analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TbRECQ2 contains a helicase domain found in helicases of multiple families.
source: Protein domain predictions (Figure 1A) suggest that TbRECQ2 contains a conserved DEAD/DEAH box helicase domain, indicating potential ATP and nucleic acid binding activity, and a more C-terminal helicase domain that is found in helicases of multiple families (Linder, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by protein domain prediction analysis shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Linder, 2006.

claim: TbRECQ2 contains an HRDC domain close to the C-terminus.
source: In addition, an HRDC (helicase and RNaseD C-terminal) domain is predicted close to the C-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by protein domain prediction analysis.

claim: The HRDC domain is limited to some RecQ helicases and RNase D homologues.
source: In contrast to the two other domains, the HRDC domain appears limited to some RecQ helicases and RNase D homologues (Morozov et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morozov et al., 1997.

claim: The HRDC domain is probably involved in DNA binding.
source: In contrast to the two other domains, the HRDC domain appears limited to some RecQ helicases and RNase D homologues (Morozov et al., 1997), where it is probably involved in DNA binding (Bachrati and Hickson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bachrati and Hickson, 2003.

claim: HRDC domains are not found in all RecQ helicases.
source: However, HRDC domains are not found in all RecQ helicases; for example, three human RecQ helicases, WRN, BLM and RECQ1, each contain an HRDC, but it is absent in human RECQ4 and RECQ5 (Bernstein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernstein et al., 2010.

claim: The RQC domain is limited to RecQ helicases.
source: One domain that is limited to RecQ helicases is termed RQC (RecQ C-terminal), which may be involved in protein-protein interactions (Bernstein et al., 2010), as well as in binding and unwinding dsDNA at branch points (Kitano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2010 and Kitano et al., 2010.

claim: The RQC domain may be involved in protein-protein interactions.
source: One domain that is limited to RecQ helicases is termed RQC (RecQ C-terminal), which may be involved in protein-protein interactions (Bernstein et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bernstein et al., 2010.

claim: The RQC domain may be involved in binding and unwinding dsDNA at branch points.
source: One domain that is limited to RecQ helicases is termed RQC (RecQ C-terminal), which may be involved in protein-protein interactions (Bernstein et al., 2010), as well as in binding and unwinding dsDNA at branch points (Kitano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kitano et al., 2010.

claim: The RQC domain could not be predicted in TbRECQ2.
source: Though this domain could not be predicted in TbRECQ2, it is also absent from or highly diverged in some other validated RecQ proteins (Bachrati and Hickson, 2003)
evidence: This is based on protein domain prediction analysis and a citation to Bachrati and Hickson, 2003.

claim: TbRECQ2 is non-essential in bloodstream form T. brucei cells.
source: The successful generation of null mutants shows TbRECQ2 is not essential in BSF T. brucei
evidence: This is supported by the successful generation of recq2-/- mutants.

claim: recq2-/- mutants have an increased population doubling time compared with WT cells.
source: The successful generation of null mutants shows TbRECQ2 is not essential in BSF T. brucei, though growth analysis revealed that the recq2-/- mutants had an increased population doubling time compared with WT cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Slowed growth is apparent in recq2+/- mutants.
source: Indeed, slowed growth was also apparent in the req2+/- mutants, suggesting a growth impediment after loss of one allele that becomes more severe in the null mutant.
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data.

claim: There is no change in the proportion of 1N1K, 1N2K or 2N2K cells in recq2 mutants relative to WT.
source: Counting the relative numbers of the two T. brucei genomes allows a cytological assessment of the cell cycle stage of individual cells in the population (McKean, 2003), and we found no change in the proportion of 1N1K (G1-S phase), 1N2K (G2-M phase) or 2N2K (post M phase) cells in mutants relative to WT (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to McKean, 2003.

claim: The growth impairment of RECQ2 mutants is not due to detectable stalling at a discernible cell cycle stage or transition.
source: Thus, the growth impairment of the RECQ2 mutants is not due to detectable stalling at a discernible cell cycle stage or transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle analysis data.

claim: γ-H2A accumulates in recq2-/- mutants.
source: Western blotting to detect the levels of Thr130 phosphorylated histone H2A (γ-H2A) revealed an increased signal in the recq2-/- mutants relative to WT (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Thr130 phosphorylation of histone H2A is a modification seen after various genotoxic treatments in T. brucei.
source: This form of phosphorylation of histone H2A is a modification seen after various genotoxic treatments in T. brucei (Glover and Horn, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glover and Horn, 2012.

claim: Accumulation of γ-H2A in recq2-/- mutants indicates an increased level of nuclear DNA damage.
source: Thus, accumulation of the histone variant in the recq2-/- mutants indicates an increased level of nuclear DNA damage, which appears not to impair cell cycle progression but may impede cell growth or survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the γ-H2A accumulation data.

claim: recq2-/- cells display much increased sensitivity to MMS compared with WT.
source: Figure 1E shows clonal survival assays, which revealed that the recq2-/- cells displayed a much increased sensitivity to MMS compared with WT.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At MMS concentrations at and above 0.0002%, recq2+/- survival is lower than WT.
source: Indeed, at MMS concentrations at and above 0.0002%, recq2+/- survival was lower than WT.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival assay data.

claim: Increased MMS sensitivity has been reported in S. cerevisiae SGS1 mutants.
source: These data are consistent with the increased MMSsensitivity previously reported in S. cerevisiae SGS1 mutants (Mullen and Brill, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mullen and Brill, 2000.

claim: Increased MMS sensitivity has been reported in human and chicken DT40 blm-/- mutants.
source: These data are consistent with the increased MMSsensitivity previously reported in S. cerevisiae SGS1 mutants (Mullen and Brill, 2000), as well as human and chicken DT40 blm-/- mutants (Imamura et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Imamura et al., 2001.

claim: TbRECQ2 is involved in the T. brucei response to MMS-induced damage.
source: These data are consistent with the increased MMSsensitivity previously reported in S. cerevisiae SGS1 mutants (Mullen and Brill, 2000), as well as human and chicken DT40 blm-/- mutants (Imamura et al., 2001), and indicate TbRECQ2 is involved in the T. brucei response to MMS-induced damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the MMS sensitivity data.

claim: TbRECQ2 contributes to the T. brucei response to phleomycin damage.
source: Clonal survival showed that TbRECQ2 also contributes to the T. brucei response to phleomycin and HU damage, since in both cases the recq2-/- mutants were more sensitive than WT cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TbRECQ2 contributes to the T. brucei response to HU damage.
source: Clonal survival showed that TbRECQ2 also contributes to the T. brucei response to phleomycin and HU damage, since in both cases the recq2-/- mutants were more sensitive than WT cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: recq2+/- cells are not clearly more sensitive than WT to phleomycin or HU.
source: However, in neither case was there clear evidence that the recq2+/- cells were more sensitive than WT, perhaps indicating a more pronounced role for the putative helicase in tackling MMS damage.
evidence: This is based on clonal survival assay data.

claim: 12myc-TbRECQ2 is expressed at the expected size (182 kDa).
source: A western blot of a cell lysate from a transformant clone showed expression of a myc-tagged protein of the expected size (182 kDa; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 12myc-TbRECQ2 is functional in repair.
source: As survival of the cells expressing only the 12myc tagged variant of TbRECQ2 was comparable with WT cells and recq2+/- mutants in the presence of MMS, and notably better than recq2-/- mutants, addition of the epitope does not impair TbRECQ2 function in repair.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 12myc-TbRECQ2 localises to subnuclear foci after exposure to phleomycin.
source: Second, TbRECQ2 protein relocalises to subnuclear foci after exposure to phleomycin and, critically, in these conditions the putative helicase displays pronounced colocalisation with TbRAD51
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 12myc-TbRECQ2 displays pronounced colocalisation with TbRAD51 after phleomycin exposure.
source: Second, TbRECQ2 protein relocalises to subnuclear foci after exposure to phleomycin and, critically, in these conditions the putative helicase displays pronounced colocalisation with TbRAD51, an enzyme that binds single-stranded DNA formed at DSBs to catalyse HR repair.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: In most cells no 12myc-TbRECQ2 signal could be detected in the absence of damage.
source: Localisation of 12myc-TbRECQ2 was examined by direct immunofluorescence with anti-myc antiserum conjugated with Alexa-Fluor 488 (Figure 2C). In most cells no signal could be detected, though in the very small proportion (0.2%) that did show a signal (Figure 2D), this was seen as a discrete puncta in the nucleus (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: 0.2% of cells show 12myc-TbRECQ2 foci in the absence of induced damage.
source: In most cells no signal could be detected, though in the very small proportion (0.2%) that did show a signal (Figure 2D), this was seen as a discrete puncta in the nucleus (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RAD51 foci are observed in ~2% of untreated cells.
source: TbRAD51 foci were observed in ~2% of untreated cells (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After growth in phleomycin, 47% of cells contained one or more 12myc-TbRECQ2 foci.
source: After growth in phleomycin, 47% of cells contained one or more 12myc-TbRECQ2 foci and 44% of cells contained one or more TbRAD51 foci (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After growth in phleomycin, 44% of cells contained one or more TbRAD51 foci.
source: After growth in phleomycin, 47% of cells contained one or more 12myc-TbRECQ2 foci and 44% of cells contained one or more TbRAD51 foci (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the majority of cells with foci (~60%), 12myc-TbRECQ2 and TbRAD51 signals co-localised fully.
source: In the majority of cells in which 12myc-TbRECQ2 and TbRAD51 foci were seen (irrespective of the number of foci), the signals co-localised fully (~60% of cells with both foci, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In ~20% of cells with foci, 12myc-TbRECQ2 and TbRAD51 signal overlap was partial.
source: In ~20% of cells with foci, the signal overlap was partial because the numbers of 12myc-TbRECQ2 and TbRAD51 foci were not equivalent in a single cell.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In ~20% of cells with foci, there was no overlap between 12myc-TbRECQ2 and TbRAD51 signals.
source: Finally, in ~20% of cells there was no overlap, because 12myc-TbRECQ2 displayed foci but TbRAD51 did not, or vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The survival rate of HR1 WT cells following I-SceI induction is ~60%.
source: The survival rate of HR1 WT cells following I-SceI induction was ~60% (Figure 3B), equivalent to that reported previously (Glover and Horn, 2014; Glover et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Glover and Horn, 2014 and Glover et al., 2008.

claim: In the absence of TbRECQ2, the survival rate of HR1 cells after I-SceI induction decreased 2-fold to ~30%.
source: In the absence of TbRECQ2, the survival rate decreased 2-fold, with only ~30% of wells displaying growth in both of the two HR1 recq2-/- clones examined.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: recq2-/- mutants are less able to survive a chromosome-internal DNA DSB than WT T. brucei cells.
source: These data indicate that recq2-/-mutants are less able to survive a chromosome-internal DNA DSB than WT T. brucei cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonal survival data after I-SceI induction in HR1 cells.

claim: All Tet-induced HR1 clones (n = 25) were puromycin sensitive.
source: Analysis of the puromycin sensitivity of surviving clones showed, for both WT and recq2-/- HR1 cells, that all Tet-induced clones (n = 25) were puromycin sensitive and all uninduced clones (n = 6) were puromycin resistant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by puromycin sensitivity data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All uninduced HR1 clones (n = 6) were puromycin resistant.
source: Analysis of the puromycin sensitivity of surviving clones showed, for both WT and recq2-/- HR1 cells, that all Tet-induced clones (n = 25) were puromycin sensitive and all uninduced clones (n = 6) were puromycin resistant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by puromycin sensitivity data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A functional PUR gene was lost in all cases after I-SceI expression was induced in HR1 cells.
source: Thus, a functional PUR gene was lost in all cases after I-SceI expression was induced, showing that DSB formation was successful and indicating repair is possible, though less efficient, in the absence of TbRECQ2.
evidence: This is inferred from the puromycin sensitivity data.

claim: The survival rate of HRES WT cells after I-SceI induction is ~24%.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Glover et al., 2013), the survival rate of HRES WT cells after I-SceI induction (~24%) was >2-fold lower than HR1 cells (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Glover et al., 2013.

claim: The survival rate of HRES WT cells after I-SceI induction is >2-fold lower than HR1 cells.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Glover et al., 2013), the survival rate of HRES WT cells after I-SceI induction (~24%) was >2-fold lower than HR1 cells (Figure 3C), indicating greater lethality when a DSB is made in the active BES.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival data shown in Figure 3C and a citation to Glover et al., 2013.

claim: The survival rate of HRES recq2-/- clones is ~50% of HRES WT cells.
source: Nonetheless, the survival rate of the two HRES recq2-/- clones (13% and 14.8%) was again ~50% of HRES WT cells, suggesting loss of TbRECQ2 impairs survival in both loci.
evidence: This is supported by clonal survival data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 14% of survivors in one HRES recq2-/- clone were puromycin resistant.
source: In fact, the level of impairment after loss of TbRECQ2 may be greater than the clonal survival assay predicts since, unlike in HR1, evaluating the puromycin sensitivity of recovered clones showed that 14% of survivors (n = 7) in one HRES recq2-/- clone and 70% (n = 10) in the other were puromycin resistant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by puromycin sensitivity data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 70% of survivors in the other HRES recq2-/- clone were puromycin resistant.
source: In fact, the level of impairment after loss of TbRECQ2 may be greater than the clonal survival assay predicts since, unlike in HR1, evaluating the puromycin sensitivity of recovered clones showed that 14% of survivors (n = 7) in one HRES recq2-/- clone and 70% (n = 10) in the other were puromycin resistant (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by puromycin sensitivity data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All puromycin sensitive HRES recq2-/- survivor clones had lost the VSG221 gene.
source: Despite this, PCR of the puromycin sensitive recq2-/- survivor clones showed that all had lost the VSG221 gene (also called VSG 427–2) (Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008) and most had retained the ESAG1 gene variant specific to the targeted BES (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3D and a citation to Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008.

claim: Most puromycin sensitive HRES recq2-/- survivor clones had retained the ESAG1 gene variant specific to the targeted BES.
source: Despite this, PCR of the puromycin sensitive recq2-/- survivor clones showed that all had lost the VSG221 gene (also called VSG 427–2) (Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008) and most had retained the ESAG1 gene variant specific to the targeted BES (Figure 3D), a pattern consistent with previous analysis in WT HRES (Glover et al., 2013) cells and relatives (Boothroyd et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3D and citations to Glover et al., 2013 and Boothroyd et al., 2009.

claim: Loss of TbRECQ2 does not result in a major shift in repair pathway after induction of a DSB in the BES.
source: Thus, loss of TbRECQ2 does not result in a major shift in repair pathway after induction of a DNA DSB in the BES, meaning reduced survival in the mutants is best explained by less efficient execution of a predominant repair reaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCR analysis of repair products.

claim: The switching rate of WT GFP221hygTK cells is ~1.5 x 10–5 cells/generation.
source: In the WT cells GCV resistant clones arose at a rate of ~1.5 x 10–5cells/generation (Figure 4B), consistent with rates determined in comparable studies Kim and Cross, 2010a, 2011a; Povelones et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data shown in Figure 4B and citations to Kim and Cross, 2010, 2011, and Povelones et al., 2012.

claim: No change in VSG switching rate was seen in recq2+/- mutants.
source: No change in rate was seen in the recq2+/- mutants (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GCV resistant cells arose around 2-fold more frequently in recq2-/- mutants (~3.2 x 10–5 resistant cells/generation).
source: No change in rate was seen in the recq2+/- mutants (Figure 4B), but GCV resistant cells arose around 2-fold more frequently in the recq2-/- mutants (~3.2 x 10–5 resistant cells/generation).
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In WT cells, most GCV resistant clones (~60%) arose by ES GC or in situ+ES del.
source: In broad agreement with observations made by Povelones et al. (2012), in WT cells most GCV resistant clones had arisen either by in ES GC or in situ+ES del (~60%), with in situ switching the next most common process (~25%); VSG GC was rare (~10%), and we found no examples of telomere XO events.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Povelones et al., 2012.

claim: In WT cells, in situ switching is the next most common VSG switching process (~25%).
source: In broad agreement with observations made by Povelones et al. (2012), in WT cells most GCV resistant clones had arisen either by in ES GC or in situ+ES del (~60%), with in situ switching the next most common process (~25%)
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Povelones et al., 2012.

claim: In WT cells, VSG GC was rare (~10%).
source: In broad agreement with observations made by Povelones et al. (2012), in WT cells most GCV resistant clones had arisen either by in ES GC or in situ+ES del (~60%), with in situ switching the next most common process (~25%); VSG GC was rare (~10%), and we found no examples of telomere XO events.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Povelones et al., 2012.

claim: No examples of telomere XO events were found in WT cells.
source: In broad agreement with observations made by Povelones et al. (2012), in WT cells most GCV resistant clones had arisen either by in ES GC or in situ+ES del (~60%), with in situ switching the next most common process (~25%); VSG GC was rare (~10%), and we found no examples of telomere XO events.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C and a citation to Povelones et al., 2012.

claim: A virtually identical pattern of VSG switching events was seen in recq2+/- cells compared to WT.
source: A virtually identical pattern of events was seen in the recq2+/- cells, consistent with the unaltered rate at which GCV resistant cells arose.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ~90% of GCV resistant clones in recq2-/- mutants arose by VSG GC (~50%) or telomere XO (~45%).
source: In contrast, ~90% of GCV resistant clones in the recq2-/- mutants arose either by VSG GC (~50% of total) or telomere XO (~45%), indicating that the elevated rate in the null mutants is due to increased use of these recombination strategies.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The elevated VSG switching rate in recq2-/- mutants is due to increased use of VSG GC and telomere XO.
source: In contrast, ~90% of GCV resistant clones in the recq2-/- mutants arose either by VSG GC (~50% of total) or telomere XO (~45%), indicating that the elevated rate in the null mutants is due to increased use of these recombination strategies.
evidence: This is inferred from the VSG switching profile data.

claim: GCV resistant cells arose ~2–3 fold less frequently in WT and recq2+/- cells in the presence of puromycin.
source: To test this interpretation further, the switching experiment was conducted in the presence of puromycin, which should prevent any events that inactivate expression of PUR (Figure 4B). In these conditions, GCV resistant cells arose ~2–3 fold less frequently in the WT and recq2+/- cells (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was less impact of puromycin on recq2-/- cells compared to WT and recq2+/- cells.
source: In these conditions, GCV resistant cells arose ~2–3 fold less frequently in the WT and recq2+/- cells (Figure 4C), consistent with their predominant use of in situ and ES GC or in situ+ES del events, whilst there was less impact on the recq2-/- cells, where VSG switching is largely downstream of PUR.
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of TbRECQ2 results in increased VSG switching by a change in repair strategy.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that loss of TbRECQ2 results in increased VSG switching by a change in repair strategy.
evidence: This is inferred from the VSG switching rate and profile data.

claim: Addition of Tet resulted in increased numbers of 1N2K cells in HR1, indicating impaired G2-M cell cycle progression.
source: However, consistent with previous reports (Glover et al., 2013; Glover and Horn, 2014; Glover et al., 2008), addition of Tet resulted in increased numbers of 1N2K cells, indicating impaired G2-M cell cycle progression (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Glover et al., 2013, Glover and Horn, 2014, and Glover et al., 2008.

claim: In HR1, 1N2K cell numbers increased to ~20% 12 hr after Tet induction and then returned to ~10% after 24 hr.
source: In HR1, 1N2K cell numbers increased (from ~10% of the uninduced population) to ~20% 12 hr after Tet induction and then returned to ~10% after 24 hr (Figure 5A), indicating the cell cycle impairment was transient.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The cell cycle impairment in HR1 after I-SceI induction was transient.
source: In HR1, 1N2K cell numbers increased (from ~10% of the uninduced population) to ~20% 12 hr after Tet induction and then returned to ~10% after 24 hr (Figure 5A), indicating the cell cycle impairment was transient.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In HRES, increased 1N2K cell numbers (~20%) persisted until 24 hr after Tet addition.
source: In contrast, increased 1N2K cell numbers (~20% of the population) persisted until 24 hr after Tet addition in HRES (Figure 5B), suggesting the response to a DSB differs if the lesion is in the active BES or a chromosome-internal site (Glover and Horn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5B and a citation to Glover and Horn, 2014.

claim: The response to a DSB differs if the lesion is in the active BES or a chromosome-internal site.
source: In contrast, increased 1N2K cell numbers (~20% of the population) persisted until 24 hr after Tet addition in HRES (Figure 5B), suggesting the response to a DSB differs if the lesion is in the active BES or a chromosome-internal site (Glover and Horn, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing cell cycle analysis data between HR1 and HRES cells and supported by a citation to Glover and Horn, 2014.

claim: In HR1, a reduction in I-SceI target PCR product was seen from 2 hr after Tet addition (20%).
source: In HR1 (Figure 5C), a reduction in product was seen from 2 hr after Tet addition (20%) and this effect increased until around 8 hr (80%), with little change in PCR efficiency thereafter (8–72 hr; Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In HR1, the reduction in I-SceI target PCR product increased until around 8 hr (80%).
source: In HR1 (Figure 5C), a reduction in product was seen from 2 hr after Tet addition (20%) and this effect increased until around 8 hr (80%), with little change in PCR efficiency thereafter (8–72 hr; Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: I-SceI cleavage in HR1 cells is rapid and reaches a maximum within a cell cycle (~8 hr).
source: These data suggest that I-SceI cleavage in HR1 cells is rapid and reaches a maximum within a cell cycle (~8 hr), an interpretation consistent with the timing of single-stranded DNA formation at I-SceI breaks detected by Southern blotting (Glover and Horn, 2014; Glover et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data and supported by citations to Glover and Horn, 2014 and Glover et al., 2008.

claim: Allelic repair products in HR1 accumulate slowly over ~16–72 hr.
source: Southern blotting suggests that allelic repair products in HR1 accumulate slowly over ~16–72 hr (Glover et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glover et al., 2008.

claim: In HRES cells, loss of I-SceI target PCR product was more rapid and more complete than in HR1, with <10% of uninduced product by 2–3 hr after Tet addition.
source: I-SceI target qPCR revealed a different response to I-SceI induction in HRES cells (Figure 5C). Early in the time course, loss of PCR product was more rapid and more complete, with <10% of uninduced product by 2–3 hr after Tet addition, suggesting I-SceI cleavage was at least as efficient in HRES cells as in HR1.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: I-SceI cleavage was at least as efficient in HRES cells as in HR1.
source: Early in the time course, loss of PCR product was more rapid and more complete, with <10% of uninduced product by 2–3 hr after Tet addition, suggesting I-SceI cleavage was at least as efficient in HRES cells as in HR1.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data.

claim: In HRES, the levels of I-SceI target PCR product increased in two distinct peaks (at ~20 and 30 hr post induction) to levels approaching that of the uninduced cells.
source: However, in contrast with HR1, the levels of PCR product later in the reaction increased, in two distinct peaks (at ~20 and 30 hr post induction), to levels approaching that of the uninduced cells.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The abundance of the VSG221 PCR product very closely matched that of the I-SceI target over the timecourse in HRES.
source: Thus, we used qPCR to ask about the fate of the BES VSG (VSG221) after I-SceI cleavage (Figure 5D). The abundance of the VSG221 PCR product very closely matched that of the I-SceI target over the timecourse
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The recurrence of VSG221 PCR product indicates the initial, rapid loss of VSG221 is not due to replacement by another VSG.
source: The abundance of the VSG221 PCR product very closely matched that of the I-SceI target over the timecourse, and the recurrence of product indicates the initial, rapid loss of VSG221 is not due to replacement by another VSG.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data.

claim: Virtually all HRES cells retained VSG221 on their surface 24 hr after Tet induction.
source: To test this further, we performed immunofluorescence with anti-VSG221 antiserum, revealing that virtually all cells retained VSG221 on their surface 24 hr after Tet induction (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Induction of a DSB by I-SceI in the active BES does not elicit rapid repair (within 32 hr) that removes the downstream VSG.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that induction of a DSB by I-SceI in the active BES does not elicit rapid repair (within 32 hr) that removes the downstream VSG.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The MFAseq pattern of peak location was invariant when comparing early S BSF and PCF cells.
source: The MFAseq pattern of peak location was invariant when comparing early S BSF and PCF cells, and when comparing late S phase BSF and PCF cells.
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The relative heights of the MFAseq peaks in each chromosome were invariant between BSF and PCF life cycle stages.
source: Even more strikingly, the relative heights of the MFAseq peaks in each chromosome were invariant between the two life cycle stages (Figure 6)
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The relative heights of the MFAseq peaks were invariant between T. brucei strains Lister427 and TREU927.
source: Even more strikingly, the relative heights of the MFAseq peaks in each chromosome were invariant between the two life cycle stages (Figure 6), as well as being invariant between T. brucei strains Lister427 and TREU927 (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data comparison (data not shown).

claim: Neither differentiation between life cycle stages nor extended growth of different T. brucei strains leads to changes in the genomic sites used as origins or changes in the timing programme of origin activation in the chromosome cores.
source: Thus, neither differentiation between life cycle stages in T. brucei, nor extended growth of different T. brucei strains, leads to changes in the genomic sites used as origins, or changes in the timing programme of origin activation in the chromosome cores.
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq data comparison.

claim: Only five origins were observed in the present data that were not predicted previously.
source: Only five origins (dashed lines, Figure 6) were observed in the present data, both in the BSF and PCF cells, which were not predicted previously (Tiengwe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 6 and a citation to Tiengwe et al., 2012.

claim: All five newly observed origins were 'weak' origins with low MFAseq peak heights.
source: All these were 'weak' origins, with low MFAseq peak heights, and it is possible that they were observed here due to the more compressed graphical representation, rather than being origins that are active in Lister 427 cells and not in TREU927.
evidence: This is based on MFAseq data analysis.

claim: The five newly observed origins localise to the boundaries of the polycistronic transcription units.
source: Using the localisation of TbORC1/CDC6 (Tiengwe et al., 2012) and histone H4K10Ac (Siegel et al., 2009) binding sites in the TREU927 genome as a guide (Figure 6), it is clear these five origins localise to the boundaries of the polycistronic transcription units, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by comparing MFAseq data with TbORC1/CDC6 and histone H4K10Ac binding sites, with citations to Tiengwe et al., 2012 and Siegel et al., 2009.

claim: There is pronounced rigidity in the coordination of nuclear DNA replication in T. brucei.
source: Taken as a whole, the above MFAseq analysis suggests pronounced rigidity in the coordination of nuclear DNA replication in T. brucei.
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq data analysis.

claim: For all but one of the BES, there was no clear difference between the MFAseq mapping in the BSF and PCF cells.
source: For all but one of the BES, there was no clear difference between the MFAseq mapping in the BSF and PCF cells, either for early or late S phase.
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There was no evidence that 13 of the 14 BES had been replicated, even in the BSF and PCF late S samples.
source: Moreover, there was no evidence that 13 of the 14 BES had been replicated, even in the BSF and PCF late S samples, since there was no consistent increase in S phase reads relative to G2: comparing the S/G2 ratios for each bin in each BES showed that the overall median S/G2 ration for most BES was ~1.0 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 13 of 14 BES are replicated very late in S phase, similar to telomeres in other eukaryotes.
source: These data suggest that 13 of 14 BES are replicated very late in S phase, similar to telomeres in other eukaryotes (Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq data and supported by a citation to Rhind and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: In BES1, BSF S phase reads (both early and late) across the BES were markedly elevated relative to G2.
source: BES1 was the single exception to the above trend. In this contig, BSF S phase reads (both early and late) across the BES were markedly elevated relative to G2 (Figure 7B), with overall median S/G2 ratios of 1.25 and 1.3 in early and late S, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: BES1 has overall median S/G2 ratios of 1.25 and 1.3 in early and late S, respectively, in BSF cells.
source: In this contig, BSF S phase reads (both early and late) across the BES were markedly elevated relative to G2 (Figure 7B), with overall median S/G2 ratios of 1.25 and 1.3 in early and late S, respectively (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The PCF MFAseq data for BES1 was comparable with all other BES, with S/G2 ratios ~1.0.
source: This effect was limited to the BSF cells, however, since the PCF MFAseq data for BES1 (again in either early or late S) was comparable with all other BES, with S/G2 ratios ~1.0 (significantly different from BSF cells: p-value < 0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by MFAseq data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: BES1, alone amongst the 14 BES, is replicated early, and this deviation from late replication is limited to mammal-infective cells.
source: These data suggest that BES1, alone amongst the 14 BES, is replicated early, and this deviation from the late replication of other BES is limited to mammal-infective cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq data comparison between BSF and PCF cells.

claim: BES1 is the actively transcribed site, encoding VSG221 in the BSF cells used in this study.
source: BES1 differs from the other BES in being the actively transcribed site, encoding VSG221 in the BSF cells used in this study, as shown by indirect immunofluorescence (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In PCF cells full transcription of all BES, including BES1, is silenced.
source: In PCF cells full transcription of all BES, including BES1, is silenced (Rudenko et al., 1994) and the VSG coat is replaced with procyclin (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rudenko et al., 1994 and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The unique early replication of BES1 only in BSF cells suggests that replication timing of T. brucei telomeres displays a precise association with transcription.
source: Thus, the unique early replication of BES1 only in BSF cells suggests that replication timing of T. brucei telomeres displays a precise association with transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq data and transcription status.

claim: qPCR of VSG221 in BES1 expressing cells revealed early and late S/G2 ratios higher than the chromosome 5 origin locus, consistent with the VSG replicating very early.
source: Furthermore, qPCR of VSG221 in the same cells revealed early and late S/G2 ratios higher than the chromosome 5 origin locus, consistent with the VSG replicating very early (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Early and late S/G2 ratios for VSG221 in BES1 TetR blockade cells were much lower than in BES1 (VSG221) expressing cells.
source: For VSG221, the early and late S/G2 ratios in the TetR blockade cells were much lower than in the BES1 (VSG221) expressing cells, being indistinguishable from the origin locus, indicating the pronounced early replication of this VSG is not seen when it is no longer transcribed.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The pronounced early replication of VSG221 is not seen when it is no longer transcribed.
source: For VSG221, the early and late S/G2 ratios in the TetR blockade cells were much lower than in the BES1 (VSG221) expressing cells, being indistinguishable from the origin locus, indicating the pronounced early replication of this VSG is not seen when it is no longer transcribed.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data.

claim: VSG121 S/G2 ratios in BES1 TetR blockade cells were higher than both VSG221 and the non-origin locus and were comparable with the origin control.
source: In contrast, in the BES1 TetR blockade cells the VSG121 S/G2 ratios were higher than both VSG221 and the non-origin locus and, instead, were comparable with the origin control (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The data suggest earlier replication of VSG121 when the VSG221-containing BES1 is silenced and BES3 is at least one of the BES expressed.
source: Thus, despite the potentially confounding effect of VSG121 array copies that may be late replicating, as well as uncertainty about the transcriptional status of all the VSG BES in these cells, these data suggest earlier replication of VSG121 when the VSG221-containing BES1 is silenced and BES3 is at least one of the BES expressed in the T. brucei population.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data.

claim: The VSG-focused qPCR experiments validate the MFAseq association between replication timing and transcription status of the telomeric BES.
source: Taken together, these VSG-focused qPCR experiments validate the MFAseq association between replication timing and transcription status of the telomeric BES.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR validation experiments.

claim: The effects of TbRECQ2 loss on VSG switching are reminiscent of the phenotypes seen after mutation of Topo3α or RMI1.
source: The effects of TbRECQ2 loss on VSG switching are reminiscent of the phenotypes seen after mutation of Topo3α or RMI1 (Kim and Cross, 2010;, 2011), providing more evidence that these factors act together in T. brucei.
evidence: This is supported by comparing the phenotypes and citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: TbRECQ2, Topo3α, and RMI1 likely act together in T. brucei.
source: The effects of TbRECQ2 loss on VSG switching are reminiscent of the phenotypes seen after mutation of Topo3α or RMI1 (Kim and Cross, 2010;, 2011), providing more evidence that these factors act together in T. brucei.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar phenotypes.

claim: VSG switching rates increase 2–3 fold in recq2-/- mutants.
source: Though VSG switching rates increase in each of the null mutants, the extent of this change is somewhat variable: a 2–3 fold increase in recq2-/- mutants, compared with 4-fold and 10–40 fold increases in rmi1 and topo3α null mutants, respectively (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching rate data and citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: VSG switching rates increase 4-fold in rmi1 null mutants.
source: Though VSG switching rates increase in each of the null mutants, the extent of this change is somewhat variable: a 2–3 fold increase in recq2-/- mutants, compared with 4-fold and 10–40 fold increases in rmi1 and topo3α null mutants, respectively (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: VSG switching rates increase 10–40 fold in topo3α null mutants.
source: Though VSG switching rates increase in each of the null mutants, the extent of this change is somewhat variable: a 2–3 fold increase in recq2-/- mutants, compared with 4-fold and 10–40 fold increases in rmi1 and topo3α null mutants, respectively (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: S. cerevisiae Sgs1 and Top3-Rmi1 can act independently on strand exchange intermediates.
source: The differing extent of VSG switching increase may be consistent with findings that S. cerevisiae Sgs1 and Top3-Rmi1 can act independently on strand exchange intermediates (Fasching et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fasching et al., 2015.

claim: The increased contribution of VSG GC and telomere XO to VSG switching is a common effect of recq2-/-, rmi1-/- and topo3α-/- mutation.
source: Irrespective of these differences, the increased contribution of VSG GC and telomere XO to VSG switching is a common effect of recq2-/- (~50% and ~40%, respectively), rmi1-/- (70% and 25%, respectively)and topo3α-/- (70% and 23%, respectively) mutation (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011).
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data and citations to Kim and Cross, 2010 and 2011.

claim: All three -/- mutants (recq2, rmi1, topo3α) display an almost complete absence of events leading to ES loss (either GC or deletion).
source: Similarly, all three -/- mutants display an almost complete absence of events leading to ES loss (either GC or deletion).
evidence: This is supported by VSG switching profile data.

claim: The increase in telomere XO in RTR mutants is consistent with the action of the RTR complex in processing recombination intermediates to suppress chromosome crossover.
source: As has been argued before (Kim and Cross, 2010; 2011), the increase in telomere XO is striking, as this effect is consistent with the action of the RTR complex in processing recombination intermediates to suppress chromosome crossover (Cejka et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Cross, 2010, 2011, and Cejka et al., 2010.

claim: Yeast Sgs1 mutation leads to increased crossover recombination after the formation of a chromosome-internal DSB.
source: In yeast, Sgs1 mutation leads to increased crossover recombination after the formation of a chromosome-internal DSB (Ira et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ira et al., 2003.

claim: The absence of crossovers in HRES recq2-/- mutants after I-SceI induction provides evidence that an induced DSB in the T. brucei active BES is tackled by a repair strategy that differs from that which directs VSG switching.
source: The absence of crossovers in HRES recq2-/- mutants after I-SceI induction provides further evidence that an induced DSB in the T. brucei active BES is tackled by a repair strategy that differs markedly from that which directs VSG switching.
evidence: This is inferred from the repair product analysis.

claim: Yeast Sgs1 mutants display increased repair by break-induced replication (BIR) at a telomere-proximal DSB.
source: Yeast Sgs1 mutants also display increased repair by break-induced replication (BIR) at a telomere-proximal DSB (Lydeard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lydeard et al., 2010.

claim: The decreased survival of HRES recq2-/- mutants after I-SceI induction indicates that an induced DSB in the active BES is inefficiently repaired by BIR.
source: The decreased survival of HRES recq2-/- mutants after I-SceI induction indicates that, perhaps surprisingly, an induced DSB in the active BES is inefficiently repaired by BIR, despite the potential for this reaction to direct VSG switching of telomeric genes (Boothroyd et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data and supported by a citation to Boothroyd et al., 2009.

claim: Inefficient engagement of a DSB in HR-mediated repair is consistent with the qPCR after I-SceI-mediated cleavage of the BES.
source: Inefficient engagement of a DSB in HR-mediated repair is consistent with the qPCR we describe after I-SceI-mediated cleavage of the BES (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data.

claim: Endonuclease cleavage, DNA DSB processing and recruitment of Rad51 occur rapidly in S. cerevisiae.
source: Targeted formation of a DSB to elicit recombination and allow temporal analysis of repair has been most extensively described in S. cerevisiae (Hicks et al., 2011; Renkawitz et al., 2013). Such studies suggest that endonuclease cleavage, DNA DSB processing and recruitment of Rad51 occur rapidly, with homology search and functional engagement of a homologous DNA substrate being slower reactions that follow from the break.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hicks et al., 2011 and Renkawitz et al., 2013.

claim: Homology search and functional engagement of a homologous DNA substrate are slower reactions that follow DSB formation in S. cerevisiae.
source: Such studies suggest that endonuclease cleavage, DNA DSB processing and recruitment of Rad51 occur rapidly, with homology search and functional engagement of a homologous DNA substrate being slower reactions that follow from the break.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hicks et al., 2011 and Renkawitz et al., 2013.

claim: The main effect of an I-SceI-induced DSB in the active BES is cell death, to a larger extent than the same lesion in the interior of chromosome 11.
source: As has been stated elsewhere (Glover et al., 2013), the main effect of an I-SceI-induced DSB in the active BES is cell death, to a larger extent than the same lesion in the interior of chromosome 11.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glover et al., 2013.

claim: I-SceI cleavage appears to be rapid in T. brucei, with a timing largely consistent with formation of single-stranded DNA, cell cycle impairment and the detection of damage by formation of either RAD51 or γH2A foci (all at around 12 hr).
source: I-SceI cleavage therefore appears to be rapid in T. brucei also, with a timing largely consistent with formation of single-stranded DNA, cell cycle impairment and the detection of damage by formation of either RAD51 or γH2A foci (all at around 12 hr) (Glover et al., 2013; Glover and Horn, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data and supported by citations to Glover et al., 2013 and Glover and Horn, 2014.

claim: Recovery of VSG switchers following induction of a DSB in the active BES may result from selection rather than rapid induction of efficient VSG-directed HR.
source: In fact, the data suggest that recovery of VSG switchers following induction of a DSB in the active BES may not result from rapid induction of efficient VSG-directed HR. Instead, switchers may be selected: i.e. most HRES cells that suffer a DSB die because repair is inefficient, and the population is gradually replaced thereafter, initially by cells in which the I-SceI site has not been cut and gradually by cells that have undergone a VSG switch that removes the I-SceI target.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR and survival data.

claim: The high rate of death after DSB formation in the active T. brucei BES may be because strand exchange is very inefficient in this setting.
source: Given the slow kinetics of repair after Rad51 loading in yeast (Hicks et al., 2011), it seems likely that the explanation for the high rate of death after DSB formation in the active T. brucei BES is that strand exchange (homology search, invasion or resolution) is very inefficient in this setting.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparison with yeast data and supported by a citation to Hicks et al., 2011.

claim: Inefficient strand exchange in the BES may reflect the limited length or level of sequence identity between VSG flanks or the complexity in searching for a repair substrate throughout the VSG archive.
source: Why this might be awaits further analysis, but it may reflect the limited length or level of sequence identity between VSG flanks (including the 70 bp repeats), or the complexity in searching for a repair substrate throughout the VSG archive.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: VSG switch initiation could be linked to DNA replication.
source: What might explain VSG switch initiation, if not the direct formation of a DSB, such as by an endonuclease? MFAseq mapping, validated by VSG-focused qPCR, provides the first evidence that initiation could be linked to DNA replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the MFAseq and qPCR data.

claim: The singular early replication of the active BES in mammal-infective T. brucei suggests a model for VSG switch initiation in which transcription of the BES allows the site to become accessible for replication and establishes conditions that generate instability.
source: As all BES are silenced and late replicating in PCF cells, the singular early replication of the active BES in mammal-infective T. brucei suggests a model for VSG switch initiation in which transcription of the BES allows the site to become accessible for replication and establishes conditions that generate instability, most likely through replication-transcription clashes within the BES (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on inference from the replication timing data.

claim: Replication-transcription clashes within the BES most likely generate instability that initiates VSG switching.
source: As all BES are silenced and late replicating in PCF cells, the singular early replication of the active BES in mammal-infective T. brucei suggests a model for VSG switch initiation in which transcription of the BES allows the site to become accessible for replication and establishes conditions that generate instability, most likely through replication-transcription clashes within the BES (Figure 9).
evidence: This is speculation based on the model proposed.

claim: Replication stalling can generate the structures that the RTR complex acts upon.
source: Replication stalling can generate the structures that the RTR complex acts upon (Cejka et al., 2010; Mankouri and Hickson, 2007), explaining the differing contributions of TbRECQ2 to VSG switching and I-SceI-induced DSB repair.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cejka et al., 2010 and Mankouri and Hickson, 2007.

claim: Stalling of replication by transcription can lead to DNA rearrangements.
source: Moreover, stalling of replication by transcription can lead to DNA rearrangements (Bermejo et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bermejo et al., 2012.

claim: Pausing of the replication fork has been shown to induce targeted mating type switching in fission yeast.
source: and pausing of the replication fork has been shown to induce targeted mating type switching in fission yeast (Klar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klar et al., 2014.
